title: Kajal Aggarwal and Shreyas Talpade Pour You a Glass of Something Toxic in 'The India Story' Teaser
excerpt: No song, no star entrance — just a number on screen and a question you can't unhear. Zee Studios' food-adulteration thriller drops its teaser and bets on dread over dazzle, in three languages on July 24.
body:
It opens not with a song, not with a star entrance, but with a number. The numbers are public, the teaser says. The consequences are visible. *Then why does the truth still feel hidden?* And just like that, **The India Story** announces itself as the rarest thing in a summer of franchise comedies and spy-universe explosions — a Hindi film that wants to make you uncomfortable.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=dXRhS-uKQO8</youtube>

The official teaser dropped this Friday, and it is a deliberate gear-change from everything else jostling for attention this week. Subtitled *Slow Poison in Progress*, the **Zee Studios** drama marks the first on-screen pairing of **Kajal Aggarwal** and **Shreyas Talpade** — and on the evidence of these ninety seconds, it's a pairing built on tension rather than chemistry. Aggarwal, so often cast for glamour, is shot here in muted, washed-out light, her usual sparkle stripped back to something harder and more watchful. Talpade plays it grim and coiled. There isn't a single frame designed to be screenshotted for a fan edit, and that's clearly the point.



> **"Aggarwal, so often cast for glamour, is shot here in muted, washed-out light, her usual sparkle stripped back to something harder and more watchful."**


The subject is food adulteration — specifically the misuse of chemicals and pesticides in farming, and the slow, invisible toll it takes on public health. Directed by **Chettan DK** and written and produced by **Sagar B Shinde**, the film reaches past the story of one family to stage what it calls a systemic national crisis: industrial negligence, corporate accountability, and the regulatory reform nobody wants to legislate. If that sounds less like a thriller and more like a public-health lecture, the teaser works overtime to prove otherwise — quick cuts, an ominous score from **Mangesh Dhakde**, and the visual language of a slow-burn conspiracy drama.

> "Kajal and Shreyas have delivered incredibly nuanced performances, and their commitment has truly elevated the film. We have worked hard to ensure that the narrative remains both engaging and impactful." — Chettan DK, director

It's a genre Bollywood has flirted with and mostly fumbled — the issue film that forgets to be a film. But the recent appetite for grounded, real-India storytelling (think the *Panchayat* and *Gram Chikitsalay* universe, or the docu-thriller wave) suggests there's a diaspora audience hungry for exactly this: stories about the India they left, told without the gloss. Food safety is a subject that travels. Every NRI parent who has lectured a visiting cousin about what's *really* in the produce back home will recognise the anxiety this teaser is mining.

The supporting cast — **Trisha Sarda**, **Murli Sharma**, **Manish Wadhwa**, **Atul Tiwari** and **Kamlesh Sawant** — leans toward character actors over headline names, another sign the makers are betting on substance over spectacle. The film was shot by DOP **Nishant Bhagwat**, with the colour grade handled at **Red Chillies Color**, which lends the teaser a surprisingly polished, cinematic finish for a socially-driven drama.

**Where and when:** *The India Story* releases in cinemas worldwide on **24 July 2026** in three languages — **Hindi, Tamil and Telugu** — as a Zee Studios global release. That tri-lingual rollout is a smart play for the diaspora: it lands the film simultaneously in front of North Indian, Tamil and Telugu audiences across the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf, rather than ghettoising it as a Hindi-only niche release. Expect the usual desi-circuit theatrical run, followed in due course by a streaming home (Zee's films typically land on **ZEE5**, with a wider OTT window likely for the diaspora markets).

Here's the take: this won't open to *Welcome To The Jungle* numbers, and it isn't trying to. It's the kind of film that lives or dies on reviews, festival buzz and the slow accumulation of word-of-mouth from viewers who walk out unsettled and start talking. The teaser is genuinely well-made — restrained where it could have been preachy, tense where it could have been dull. Whether the full film can sustain that for two hours is the open question.

But in a week wall-to-wall with sequels and spy crossovers, a thriller that asks what's actually in your dinner is, at the very least, the most interesting thing in the room. Mark July 24. This one might creep up on you — slowly, like the poison it's named for.
